en.title: Nursing: the whole course
en.short: What nursing is, how nursing degrees and college programmes are organised, and how to study them safely.

sections.heading: What nursing is
sections.text:
Nursing is the protection and promotion of health, the prevention of illness, and the care of people who are sick, disabled or dying. Nurses work with individuals, families and communities, of all ages and in all settings. They also act as advocates for patients. Nursing is a profession with its own body of knowledge, its own ethical code and its own legal regulation. It is not simply assistance to doctors.

These summaries teach concepts for learning and revision. They are not clinical advice, and they give no drug doses and no instructions for treating anyone. Guidelines, laws and protocols differ between countries and they change. In practice, follow your current local protocols and the supervision of qualified staff. Anyone who is unwell or in crisis should seek local medical help.

sections.heading: How programmes are organised
sections.text:
Routes into nursing differ between countries, and a regulator approves each route. In Nigeria, a Bachelor of Nursing Science (BNSc) at university usually takes five years. Schools and colleges of nursing offer programmes that lead to registration as a nurse or midwife. Many colleges now run National Diploma and Higher National Diploma (ND and HND) nursing programmes with approval from the National Board for Technical Education, and these arrangements are still changing. The Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria (NMCN) sets standards and registers practitioners. In Ghana, Kenya, South Africa and the UK, national councils play a similar part. Always check current rules with your own regulator.

Most programmes join classroom teaching to supervised clinical placements. Placements usually carry a large share of the course, and many regulators require a set number of practice hours or a professional examination.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The first stage builds foundations. It covers the nature of nursing and its theories, the nursing process, anatomy and physiology, infection prevention, health assessment, fundamental care and communication.

The middle stage applies these to clinical areas. It includes pharmacology and safe medicine administration, medical-surgical nursing, care of deteriorating patients, palliative care, maternal and child health, midwifery basics, paediatric nursing, mental health nursing, and community and public health nursing. Ethics, law, patient safety and leadership run through all of this.

Master’s study moves to advanced practice, evidence-based nursing and research methods. Students learn to judge evidence, lead improvement and contribute new knowledge.

sections.heading: How to study nursing
sections.text:
Connect each subject to a person. When you learn a condition, ask what the patient would feel, what you would observe, what could go wrong and whom you would tell. This is called clinical reasoning, and it is what examiners and clinical teachers look for.

Learn normal physiology before disease, because abnormal findings only make sense against normal ones. Use the nursing process as a framework for answering case questions. Practise skills in the skills laboratory before placement, and ask your supervisor for feedback. Reflect after placement on what happened and what you would change. Keep a list of the official guidelines used in your country, and check their dates.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Many students memorise lists without the reasons behind them, and then cannot adapt to an unfamiliar case. Some treat a task as finished once it is done, and forget to evaluate the result. Others write vague records, such as saying that a patient is fine, rather than recording what was observed and when.

In medicine rounds, a common error is to rely on memory rather than checking the prescription, the patient and the label each time. In examinations, candidates often leave out safety, escalation, consent and documentation. Another mistake is to quote one country’s law or guideline as if it applied everywhere. A serious mistake is to use study notes like these to treat yourself, relatives or friends. Clinical decisions need a qualified professional who can assess the person directly.

keyPoints: Nursing is an autonomous, regulated profession as well as a collaborative one.
The nursing process is the framework for most clinical thinking.
Rules and guidelines vary between countries and change over time.
Safety, consent, escalation and records belong in almost every answer.
These notes teach concepts and do not replace local protocols or clinical supervision.

en.title: Nursing as a profession: history and theory
en.short: How modern nursing developed, what nurses do, and the main theories used to explain nursing.

sections.heading: How modern nursing developed
sections.text:
People have always cared for the sick, often within families and religious communities. Modern nursing is usually traced to the 1850s and the Crimean War. Florence Nightingale improved sanitation and record keeping in military hospitals, and she used statistics to argue for reform. Her book Notes on Nursing appeared in 1859, and her training school opened at St Thomas’ Hospital in London in 1860. Mary Seacole, a Jamaican-born nurse, also cared for soldiers in that war. Many other traditions of care existed across Africa and Asia, and nursing in each country has its own history of training and leadership.

Today nursing is a graduate profession in many countries. Nurses act as caregivers, educators, advocates, managers and researchers.

sections.heading: What a theory does
sections.text: A nursing theory is an organised way of explaining what nursing is and how it should be done. Many writers describe four central ideas, called the metaparadigm: the person, the environment, health and nursing. Theories help nurses decide what to assess and why they act.

sections.heading: Some important theorists
sections.text:
Florence Nightingale stressed the environment: clean air, clean water, light and quiet help the body to recover.
Virginia Henderson described 14 basic needs, such as breathing and eating. The nurse helps the person with what they cannot yet do alone.
Dorothea Orem wrote the self-care deficit theory. Nursing is needed when a person’s ability to care for themselves falls below what they need.
Hildegard Peplau focused on the relationship between nurse and patient, which passes through phases over time.
Callista Roy saw people as adapting to change, and nursing as supporting that adaptation.

For example, Orem’s theory fits a man newly diagnosed with diabetes. The nurse first does more for him, then teaches him until he can manage his own care.

keyPoints: Modern nursing is usually traced to the reforms of the 1850s.
The metaparadigm is person, environment, health and nursing.
Henderson described 14 basic needs.
Orem’s theory centres on self-care deficit.
Peplau’s theory centres on the nurse-patient relationship.

en.title: The nursing process
en.short: The five steps of assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation and evaluation, with a worked care plan.

sections.heading: Five linked steps
sections.text:
The nursing process is a systematic method for planning and giving individual care. It is a cycle, because evaluation leads back to new assessment.
Assessment: collect subjective data, which the person tells you, and objective data, which you observe or measure.
Diagnosis: decide what the person’s health problems and risks are.
Planning: set priorities and goals with the person.
Implementation: carry out the planned care.
Evaluation: check whether the goals were met, and change the plan if they were not.

sections.heading: Nursing diagnosis and goals
sections.text:
A medical diagnosis names a disease, such as pneumonia. A nursing diagnosis names a human response that nurses can act on, such as difficulty clearing the airway. NANDA International publishes one widely used list, but not every country or school uses it. A common format states the problem, its cause and the evidence.

Goals should be centred on the patient and measurable. Many courses use the word SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. Priorities are often set using airway, breathing and circulation first, then Maslow’s hierarchy of needs.

sections.heading: A worked example
sections.text:
Kwame had abdominal surgery yesterday. He says his pain is 7 out of 10 and he avoids coughing. His breathing is shallow.
Diagnosis: ineffective breathing pattern related to wound pain, shown by shallow breaths and reluctance to cough.
Goal: within 24 hours, Kwame will take deep breaths and cough with pain at a level he finds acceptable.
Implementation: assess pain regularly, give analgesia as prescribed, support the wound with a pillow when he coughs, teach deep breathing, help him to sit up and walk as the plan allows.
Evaluation: the next day, reassess his pain, breathing and chest sounds. Record the result and update the plan.

The steps stay the same in every setting, including the home and the clinic. The details follow local protocols and the person’s own wishes.

keyPoints: The five steps are assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation and evaluation.
Subjective data come from the person; objective data are observed or measured.
A nursing diagnosis describes a response, not a disease.
Goals should be measurable and agreed with the person.
Evaluation leads back to reassessment.

en.title: Anatomy and physiology: homeostasis, nerves and hormones
en.short: How the body is organised, how it keeps stable, and how nerves and hormones control it.

sections.heading: Levels and stability
sections.text:
The body is organised from cells to tissues, organs and systems. Anatomy describes structure, and physiology describes function. Nurses use both to understand what they observe.

Homeostasis is the keeping of a stable internal state, such as a core temperature near 37 °C. Most control uses negative feedback. A sensor detects a change, a control centre responds, and an effector reverses the change. For example, when body temperature rises, the hypothalamus triggers sweating and widens skin blood vessels. Heat is lost, and temperature falls. Illness often reflects failure of this control, or the strain of maintaining it. A fast pulse in a bleeding patient is the body trying to maintain blood flow.

sections.heading: The nervous system
sections.text:
The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord. The peripheral nervous system includes 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves. Neurons carry electrical signals and pass them across synapses using chemical neurotransmitters.

The autonomic nervous system controls involuntary functions. Its sympathetic division prepares the body for stress: the heart rate rises, the airways widen and the pupils dilate. Its parasympathetic division supports rest and digestion. This explains many clinical signs. A person in shock may have pale, sweaty skin and a fast pulse because of sympathetic activity.

sections.heading: The endocrine system
sections.text:
Endocrine glands release hormones into the blood. Hormones act more slowly than nerves, but their effects often last longer. The pituitary gland controls several other glands. The thyroid gland influences metabolic rate. The adrenal glands make cortisol, aldosterone and adrenaline. The pancreas makes insulin, which lowers blood glucose, and glucagon, which raises it.

Blood glucose shows negative feedback clearly. After a meal, glucose rises and insulin is released, so cells take up glucose and the level falls. Between meals, glucagon helps release stored glucose. Failure of this system is the basis of diabetes mellitus.

keyPoints: Homeostasis keeps the internal environment stable.
Negative feedback reverses a change.
The sympathetic system prepares the body for stress.
Insulin lowers blood glucose and glucagon raises it.
Many clinical signs are the body’s attempts to compensate.

en.title: Anatomy and physiology: heart, lungs, kidneys and blood
en.short: How circulation, breathing, the kidneys and blood work, as a basis for nursing observation.

sections.heading: Heart and circulation
sections.text:
The heart has four chambers. The right side pumps blood to the lungs, and the left side pumps it to the body. Valves keep the flow moving in one direction. Cardiac output is the volume of blood pumped each minute.

Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate.
Example: 70 mL × 70 beats per minute = 4,900 mL per minute, or about 4.9 L per minute.

Blood pressure depends on cardiac output and on the resistance of blood vessels. When blood volume falls, the heart rate often rises first, and blood pressure may stay normal for a time. A normal blood pressure therefore does not rule out serious blood loss.

sections.heading: Breathing and gas exchange
sections.text: Air travels through the trachea and bronchi to the alveoli, the tiny air sacs of the lungs. Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the thin alveolar wall by diffusion. Most oxygen in blood is carried on haemoglobin in red blood cells. The main stimulus to breathe in healthy people is the level of carbon dioxide in the blood, detected by chemoreceptors. A rising respiratory rate is often one of the earliest signs that a patient is becoming unwell.

sections.heading: Kidneys
sections.text: Each kidney contains about one million nephrons. A nephron filters blood at the glomerulus, then reabsorbs useful substances such as water and glucose, and secretes wastes. The kidneys control water, electrolytes and acid-base balance. They also help control blood pressure through the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and they make erythropoietin, which stimulates the production of red blood cells. Low urine output can be an early warning of poor blood flow to the kidneys.

sections.heading: Blood
sections.text: Blood contains plasma, red cells, white cells and platelets. Red cells carry oxygen, white cells fight infection and platelets help clotting. Anaemia means too little haemoglobin, so less oxygen reaches the tissues. Nurses see its effects as tiredness, breathlessness and pallor.

keyPoints: Cardiac output equals stroke volume multiplied by heart rate.
The right heart pumps to the lungs and the left heart to the body.
Gas exchange happens in the alveoli by diffusion.
The nephron filters, reabsorbs and secretes.
A raised respiratory rate is an important early warning sign.

en.title: Infection prevention and control
en.short: The chain of infection, standard precautions, hand hygiene and how infection spreads in health care.

sections.heading: The chain of infection
sections.text: Infection spreads through six links: an infectious agent, a reservoir, a portal of exit, a mode of transmission, a portal of entry and a susceptible host. Breaking any link can stop the spread. A healthcare-associated infection is one that a person acquires while receiving care, such as a catheter-related urinary infection or a surgical wound infection. Many of these infections can be prevented.

sections.heading: Standard and transmission-based precautions
sections.text:
Standard precautions apply to all patients in all settings, whether or not an infection is known. They include hand hygiene, personal protective equipment (PPE) chosen by risk, respiratory hygiene, safe handling of sharps, clean equipment and surroundings, safe handling of linen and safe waste disposal.

Transmission-based precautions are added for known or suspected infections. They are grouped by route: contact, droplet and airborne. For example, airborne precautions are used for pulmonary tuberculosis.

The World Health Organization (WHO) describes five moments for hand hygiene:
Before touching a patient.
Before a clean or aseptic procedure.
After a risk of exposure to body fluids.
After touching a patient.
After touching a patient’s surroundings.

Alcohol-based hand rub is suitable for most moments. Soap and water are needed when hands are visibly dirty, and for some organisms such as those that form spores. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene.

sections.heading: Asepsis, cleaning and sharps
sections.text:
Asepsis means keeping harmful organisms away from a vulnerable site. Equipment is made safe by cleaning, disinfection or sterilisation, according to the risk of its use.

Used needles should not be recapped by hand, and they go straight into a sharps container. A needlestick injury should be reported at once, because time-sensitive care may be needed under the local protocol. Waste colour codes and policies differ between countries. Follow your facility’s current policy.

keyPoints: The chain of infection has six links.
Standard precautions apply to every patient.
Precautions by route are contact, droplet and airborne.
WHO names five moments for hand hygiene.
Gloves do not replace hand hygiene.
Report a sharps injury immediately.

en.title: Health assessment and vital signs
en.short: Taking a nursing history, physical assessment skills, and what vital signs mean.

sections.heading: History and physical assessment
sections.text:
A nursing history records the person’s main concerns, past illnesses, medicines, allergies, family and social background, and daily activities. Allergies should always be recorded clearly. Use open questions first, and speak to the person directly where possible.

Physical assessment uses four skills: inspection, palpation (touch), percussion (tapping) and auscultation (listening). Skin colour changes can be harder to see on darker skin. Look at the inner lips, the conjunctiva and the nail beds for pallor or cyanosis. Pulse oximeters may also overestimate oxygen levels in people with darker skin, so read the number alongside the whole picture.

sections.heading: Vital signs
sections.text:
Commonly quoted ranges for a resting adult are:
Temperature: about 36 to 37.5 °C, depending on site and source.
Pulse: 60 to 100 beats per minute.
Respiratory rate: 12 to 20 breaths per minute.
Oxygen saturation: usually 95% or above in healthy adults.
Blood pressure: many guidelines define hypertension from about 140/90 mmHg, but thresholds differ.

These ranges are guides and not rules. Children have different normal values. Athletes and older adults may differ too. Your facility’s chart and your country’s guideline apply. Count breaths for a full minute, ideally without telling the person, because breathing changes when people are watched. Feel the pulse for rate, rhythm and strength. Choose the correct cuff size for blood pressure, because a wrong size gives a wrong reading.

sections.heading: Reading the trend
sections.text: A single reading matters less than the pattern. For example, Ngozi’s pulse rises from 84 to 96 and then 112 over four hours, and her respiratory rate rises from 16 to 24. Each number alone may seem acceptable, but together they suggest deterioration. The nurse should repeat the observations, look at the patient and report promptly. Pain is also assessed, often with a scale from 0 to 10, and a person’s own report is the main guide.

keyPoints: Record allergies clearly in every assessment.
The four physical skills are inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation.
Look at inner lips and nail beds for colour changes on darker skin.
Normal ranges are guides and differ with age.
Trends often matter more than a single reading.

en.title: Fundamental nursing care
en.short: Hygiene, skin, mobility, nutrition and elimination: the daily care that prevents harm.

sections.heading: Why basic care matters
sections.text: Fundamental care means meeting the needs a person normally meets alone: washing, eating, drinking, moving, using the toilet and sleeping. This care protects dignity and gives the nurse time to observe. While washing a patient, a nurse may notice a new rash, a sore heel or a change in mood. Always explain what you will do, ask for consent, close the curtain and encourage the person to do what they can.

sections.heading: Skin and mobility
sections.text:
A pressure injury, also called a pressure ulcer, is damage to skin and deeper tissue caused by pressure, often with shear. It usually occurs over bony areas such as the sacrum and heels. Risk increases with immobility, poor nutrition, moisture and reduced sensation. Tools such as the Braden and Waterlow scales help to assess risk. Prevention includes regular repositioning, skin checks, moisture control and good nutrition. On darker skin, redness can be hard to see, so also feel for changes in warmth and firmness.

Immobility can also cause chest infection, clots in the leg veins, muscle wasting and stiff joints. Falls are a major hazard. Safe moving and handling protects both patient and nurse, and each facility should have its own policy and equipment.

sections.heading: Nutrition, fluids and elimination
sections.text:
Illness often reduces appetite, and poor nutrition slows healing. Screening tools identify people at risk. Nurses monitor intake, help with feeding, and check for swallowing problems. A person with a swallowing difficulty should be referred for assessment, because food or fluid may enter the lungs, which is called aspiration.

Elimination is a private need that people may find hard to discuss. Nurses observe urine and stool, and they support continence. A urinary catheter increases the risk of infection, so it should be used only when needed and should be removed as soon as it is no longer needed. Good mouth care prevents pain and infection, and it also helps patients to eat and speak.

keyPoints: Basic care protects dignity and allows observation.
Pressure injuries form over bony areas.
Check warmth and firmness as well as colour on darker skin.
Immobility affects the lungs, the veins, muscles and joints.
Remove urinary catheters as soon as they are not needed.

en.title: Communication and documentation
en.short: Therapeutic communication, teaching patients, handover with SBAR, and keeping good records.

sections.heading: Therapeutic communication
sections.text:
Therapeutic communication is purposeful communication that supports the patient. It includes active listening, open questions, silence, summarising and empathy. Empathy means trying to understand how another person feels, and showing that you have understood. False reassurance, such as saying that everything will be fine, closes the conversation and may not be true.

Barriers include pain, hearing loss, fear, noise, hierarchy and language. A trained interpreter is preferred over a relative where one is available, because relatives may change the message and the patient may not speak freely. Respect cultural and religious preferences, but do not assume them. Ask.

The teach-back method checks understanding. The nurse asks the person to explain the instructions in their own words. This tests the teaching, not the patient.

sections.heading: Handover with SBAR
sections.text:
Many errors begin with poor communication between staff. SBAR is a structured way to pass on information clearly: Situation, Background, Assessment and Recommendation.

Example of a call to a doctor:
Situation: This is Fatima, the nurse on Ward 4. I am calling about Mr Okoro in Bed 6, who is breathless.
Background: He had a hip operation two days ago.
Assessment: His respiratory rate is 28, his pulse is 118, and he looks worse than an hour ago.
Recommendation: I would like you to review him now.

sections.heading: Documentation
sections.text:
Records support continuity of care and they are legal documents. Good records are factual, accurate, written at the time or soon after, legible, dated, timed and signed. Record what you saw, did and said, and how the person responded. Avoid vague words and unapproved abbreviations. Never alter a record so that the earlier entry cannot be read. Follow your facility’s rule for correcting errors.

Confidentiality applies to paper, electronic records and conversation. Do not discuss patients in public places or post about them on social media. Share information only with those who need it for care, or where the law requires it.

keyPoints: Open questions and active listening are core skills.
Avoid false reassurance.
Use trained interpreters where possible.
SBAR means Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation.
Records must be factual, dated, timed and signed.
Teach-back checks whether the teaching worked.

en.title: Pharmacology principles for nurses
en.short: How medicines move through and act on the body, and why people respond differently.

sections.heading: What the body does to a medicine
sections.text:
Pharmacokinetics describes the movement of a medicine through the body. It has four stages, often remembered as ADME:
Absorption: entry into the blood.
Distribution: travel to the tissues.
Metabolism: chemical change, mainly in the liver.
Excretion: removal, mainly by the kidneys.

The route affects absorption. A medicine given by mouth passes through the liver before it reaches the general circulation, and some of it may be broken down. This is called first-pass metabolism. A medicine given into a vein enters the blood directly and acts quickly, so an error can cause harm quickly too. Half-life is the time taken for the blood level to fall by half. It helps to explain why some medicines are given more often than others.

sections.heading: What a medicine does to the body
sections.text: Pharmacodynamics describes the effects of medicines. Many act on receptors. An agonist activates a receptor, and an antagonist blocks it. Others act on enzymes or on microorganisms. The therapeutic index compares the amount that helps with the amount that harms. A medicine with a narrow therapeutic index needs extra care, because the gap between a useful level and a dangerous level is small.

sections.heading: Why responses differ
sections.text:
Age, body size, pregnancy, breastfeeding, genetics, and liver or kidney disease all change how medicines behave. Babies and older adults often handle medicines differently from other adults. An adverse drug reaction is an unwanted and harmful response. Some are predictable from the medicine’s action, and others, such as allergy, are not. An interaction occurs when one substance changes the effect of another. Herbal remedies and food can also interact, so always ask about them without judgement.

A medicine has a generic name and often several brand names. Nurses should learn generic names, because one medicine can appear under different labels. Antimicrobial resistance is a global concern, and nurses help by supporting appropriate use. Doses and approvals change and differ between countries, so always use your current national formulary. These notes do not give doses.

keyPoints: ADME means absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion.
An agonist activates a receptor and an antagonist blocks it.
A narrow therapeutic index needs extra care.
Age, pregnancy and organ disease change how medicines behave.
Always ask about herbal remedies and allergies.
Use the current national formulary for dose information.

en.title: Safe medicine administration
en.short: The rights of medication administration, high-alert medicines and how to prevent and report errors.

sections.heading: The rights of administration
sections.text:
The classic five rights are the right patient, right medicine, right dose, right route and right time. Many courses add the right documentation, right reason, right response, and the person’s right to information and to refuse. The rights are a framework, but they do not guarantee safety alone, because errors also come from the system around the nurse.

Good practice includes checking the prescription and allergy status, identifying the person using at least two identifiers, checking the label and the expiry date, and recording the medicine at once. Do not give a medicine you do not understand. If a prescription is unclear or seems wrong, question it with the prescriber or pharmacist before giving it. A person has the right to refuse: explore why, then record and report.

sections.heading: Calculations and high-alert medicines
sections.text:
Medicine calculations must be checked and must be sensible. Courses teach a general formula: the amount prescribed, divided by the strength available, multiplied by the volume it comes in. Convert to the same unit first. For example, 1 g = 1,000 mg, and 1 mg = 1,000 micrograms. A misplaced decimal point can cause a tenfold error. If the answer seems unusual, stop and check.

High-alert medicines can cause serious harm if used wrongly. Examples include insulin, anticoagulants, opioids and concentrated electrolytes. Facilities often require an independent second check. Look-alike and sound-alike names cause errors, and interruptions make them more likely.

sections.heading: Errors and reporting
sections.text: If an error occurs, first check the person and get help, then tell the responsible staff and report it under local policy. Be honest with the patient. Reporting helps the system to learn. WHO launched Medication Without Harm in 2017, with the aim of cutting severe, avoidable medicine-related harm. Suspected adverse reactions and falsified medicines should be reported to the national regulator, such as NAFDAC in Nigeria or the MHRA in the UK. Local protocols, scope-of-practice rules and formularies apply, and they change.

keyPoints: The classic rights are patient, medicine, dose, route and time.
Check allergies and use at least two identifiers.
Question any prescription that is unclear.
Convert to the same unit before calculating.
High-alert medicines often need an independent second check.
Report errors honestly and promptly.

en.title: Medical-surgical nursing: care around surgery
en.short: Nursing before, during and after surgery, the WHO checklist, and common postoperative complications.

sections.heading: Before and during surgery
sections.text:
Perioperative care covers the time before, during and after an operation. Preoperative care includes assessment, teaching and preparation. The nurse checks that identity, the procedure, any site marking, allergies, investigations and fasting instructions are in order, and that any regular medicines have been reviewed. Fasting rules and preparation depend on local protocols. Consent should be obtained by a person qualified to explain the procedure. The nurse may check that the form is complete and speak up if the person seems not to understand.

In the operating theatre, the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist has three pauses: before anaesthesia (sign in), before the skin incision (time out) and before the patient leaves the theatre (sign out). The team confirms key points aloud. This improves communication and reduces avoidable harm.

sections.heading: After surgery
sections.text: Immediately after surgery, the priorities are airway, breathing and circulation. Nurses monitor vital signs, level of consciousness, pain, the wound and any drains, urine output, fluid balance and nausea. Good pain control helps a patient to breathe deeply and move, which prevents complications.

sections.heading: Complications and healing
sections.text:
Common complications include:
Bleeding and shock: fast pulse, low blood pressure, cold skin.
Chest problems: collapse of small airways or pneumonia, with shallow breathing and fever.
Venous thromboembolism: a clot in a leg vein that can travel to the lung.
Wound infection: redness, heat, swelling, pus or fever.
Ileus: the bowel temporarily stops moving, causing bloating and vomiting.

A wound heals by primary intention when its edges are closed, and by secondary intention when it is left open to fill from below. Healing depends on blood supply, nutrition, infection and diseases such as diabetes. Early movement, breathing exercises and clot-prevention plans are common elements of recovery programmes, and they follow the surgical team’s instructions. Any sudden change in a patient should be reported without delay.

keyPoints: The WHO checklist has sign in, time out and sign out.
After surgery, check airway, breathing and circulation first.
Good pain control helps movement and breathing.
Bleeding, chest problems, clots and infection are key complications.
Wounds heal by primary or secondary intention.

en.title: Medical-surgical nursing: heart and lungs
en.short: Nursing concepts for hypertension, heart failure, stroke, asthma, COPD and pneumonia.

sections.heading: Heart and circulation
sections.text:
Hypertension is persistently raised blood pressure. It often causes no symptoms, and it increases the risk of stroke, heart disease and kidney disease. It is a major problem across Africa and worldwide. Nurses measure blood pressure, support lifestyle change and help people to continue long-term treatment.

Heart failure means the heart cannot pump enough blood for the body’s needs. Left-sided failure tends to cause breathlessness because fluid builds up in the lungs. Right-sided failure tends to cause swollen legs and a swollen liver. Nurses monitor weight, fluid balance and breathing, and they teach people to recognise worsening.

Acute coronary syndrome occurs when blood flow to heart muscle is suddenly reduced. Chest pain, breathlessness or sweating needs urgent assessment. Stroke is a sudden loss of brain function, due to a blocked or bleeding blood vessel. Many campaigns use FAST: Face, Arms, Speech, Time. Treatment can depend on time, so people need to reach hospital quickly.

sections.heading: Lungs
sections.text:
Asthma is a long-term condition with reversible narrowing of the airways. Triggers include dust, smoke and exercise. Nurses teach inhaler technique, and they check it regularly, because poor technique is a common reason for poor control.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) causes lasting airflow limitation. Tobacco is a main cause, and smoke from indoor cooking fires is an important cause in many countries. Pneumonia is an infection of the lung tissue, shown by fever, cough, fast breathing and sometimes confusion in older people.

sections.heading: Nursing principles
sections.text: Oxygen is a medicine. It should be given according to prescription or local protocol, with monitoring, and the target range depends on the person. Some people with long-term lung disease need a lower target. Positioning, usually sitting upright, can ease breathing. Treatment guidelines vary and they are updated often, so use your current national guideline. Teaching, follow-up and support to continue care matter in every long-term condition.

keyPoints: Hypertension is often silent.
Left-sided heart failure mainly affects the lungs.
FAST means Face, Arms, Speech, Time.
Check inhaler technique regularly.
Oxygen is a medicine with a target range.

en.title: Medical-surgical nursing: fluids, electrolytes and the kidneys
en.short: Body fluid compartments, electrolytes, fluid balance charts, and acute and chronic kidney disease.

sections.heading: Fluids and electrolytes
sections.text:
Water makes up a little over half of an adult’s body weight. About two-thirds of it lies inside cells and one-third lies outside. Sodium is the main electrolyte in fluid outside cells. Potassium is the main electrolyte inside cells, and it is vital for the heart. Both high and low potassium can cause dangerous heart rhythm problems. Electrolyte results should be reported according to local policy.

Dehydration may cause thirst, dry mouth, a fast pulse, dark or reduced urine and low blood pressure. Fluid overload may cause swelling, breathlessness and weight gain. Older adults, young children and people with kidney or heart disease are at greater risk of both.

sections.heading: A fluid balance chart
sections.text:
A fluid balance chart records all that goes in and all that comes out over a set time. It works only if each entry is accurate and timely. Daily weight, where available, is a useful check.

Example for 24 hours:
In: 1,200 mL by mouth + 900 mL into a vein = 2,100 mL.
Out: 1,400 mL urine + 250 mL from a drain = 1,650 mL.
Balance: 2,100 − 1,650 = +450 mL, which is a positive balance.

The chart does not count fluid lost through the skin and lungs, or some fluid lost by fever and diarrhoea. Interpret it alongside the patient’s condition.

sections.heading: Kidney disease
sections.text:
Acute kidney injury is a sudden fall in kidney function, often over hours or days. Common causes are low blood flow to the kidneys, such as in severe dehydration or sepsis, and certain medicines. It may recover if the cause is treated quickly.

Chronic kidney disease is long-lasting damage, commonly linked with diabetes and hypertension. It may progress to kidney failure, which requires dialysis or transplant. Nurses monitor blood pressure, urine output and blood results, support diet plans and help to protect veins for dialysis access. Access to dialysis varies widely between and within countries, and care plans must take account of this.

keyPoints: About two-thirds of body water lies inside cells.
Abnormal potassium can cause dangerous heart rhythms.
Fluid balance equals total in minus total out.
Daily weight is a useful check on fluid balance.
Diabetes and hypertension are common causes of chronic kidney disease.

en.title: Medical-surgical nursing: diabetes
en.short: The types of diabetes, high and low blood glucose, long-term complications and supporting self-care.

sections.heading: Types of diabetes
sections.text: Diabetes mellitus is a long-term condition with raised blood glucose. In type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys the insulin-making cells of the pancreas, so the body produces little or no insulin. In type 2 diabetes, the body responds poorly to insulin and may not make enough. Type 2 is far more common and is often linked with weight, inactivity, age and family history. Gestational diabetes first appears during pregnancy. Diagnosis uses blood tests such as fasting glucose or HbA1c, which reflects average glucose over about two to three months. Diagnostic values are set in national and international guidelines.

sections.heading: Acute problems
sections.text:
Hypoglycaemia means low blood glucose. It may cause sweating, shaking, hunger, confusion and eventually loss of consciousness. It can develop quickly and it is an emergency. Facilities have a protocol for treating it, and nurses should know it.

Hyperglycaemia means high blood glucose. It may cause thirst, frequent urination, tiredness and blurred vision. Diabetic ketoacidosis is a dangerous complication, more typical in type 1 diabetes, in which the body burns fat and the blood becomes acidic. It may cause vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing and drowsiness. Infection is a common trigger. It needs urgent hospital care.

sections.heading: Long-term care
sections.text:
Over years, raised glucose damages blood vessels and nerves. This can affect the eyes, the kidneys, the heart and the feet. Reduced feeling in the feet means that a small wound may go unnoticed, and poor circulation slows healing. Regular foot checks by the person and by health workers help to prevent ulcers and amputations.

The nurse’s main role is education and support for self-care. For example, Thandi has type 2 diabetes and works long shifts. The nurse helps her to fit meals, activity, monitoring and clinic visits into her real life, considering food customs and cost. Insulin is a high-alert medicine, and devices, treatment plans and targets vary, so these follow the current national guideline and the care team.

keyPoints: Type 1 means little or no insulin; type 2 means poor response to insulin.
HbA1c reflects glucose over about two to three months.
Hypoglycaemia is an emergency that can develop quickly.
Ketoacidosis needs urgent hospital care.
Foot care helps to prevent ulcers and amputation.

en.title: Nursing and communicable diseases: malaria, HIV and TB
en.short: Concepts for malaria, HIV and tuberculosis, with the nurse’s role in prevention, testing and adherence.

sections.heading: Malaria
sections.text: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites and spread by the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. Plasmodium falciparum causes most deaths, especially in young children and in pregnancy, and most deaths occur in Africa. Fever can lead quickly to severe disease. WHO advises confirming malaria with a test before treatment wherever possible. Prevention includes insecticide-treated nets, indoor spraying, preventive medicines in some groups and, since 2021, malaria vaccines for children in areas of risk. Nurses teach prevention and watch for danger signs, such as convulsions, confusion, severe anaemia or breathing difficulty.

sections.heading: HIV
sections.text: HIV attacks the immune system, especially CD4 cells. Without treatment it can progress to AIDS. It spreads through certain body fluids: by unprotected sex, by blood, and from mother to child during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding. It does not spread by casual contact. Antiretroviral therapy suppresses the virus, and a person with a sustained undetectable viral load does not pass HIV to sexual partners. Nurses provide confidential counselling and testing, support adherence, and help to prevent mother-to-child transmission. Post-exposure care is time-sensitive and follows local protocol.

sections.heading: Tuberculosis
sections.text: Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and it usually affects the lungs. It spreads through the air, in tiny particles, when a person with lung TB coughs. Typical symptoms are a cough lasting more than two weeks, fever, night sweats and weight loss. Molecular tests, such as Xpert, are widely used in diagnosis. Treatment lasts months and uses several medicines together. Stopping early can lead to drug-resistant disease, so support for adherence is central to nursing.

sections.heading: Principles across these diseases
sections.text: Stigma keeps people from testing and treatment. Nurses should speak without blame, protect confidentiality and work with the person’s family only as the person agrees. In outbreaks, such as Lassa fever in West Africa, nurses are at risk too, so infection prevention and early reporting are vital. Medicines and regimens change as evidence grows, so use your current national guideline.

keyPoints: WHO advises testing for malaria before treatment wherever possible.
Falciparum malaria causes most malaria deaths.
HIV does not spread through casual contact.
Sustained undetectable viral load prevents sexual transmission of HIV.
A cough lasting over two weeks should prompt TB assessment.
Stopping TB treatment early can cause drug resistance.

en.title: Recognising the deteriorating patient
en.short: Early warning signs, the ABCDE approach, shock and sepsis, and how to escalate care.

sections.heading: A structured approach
sections.text:
Patients often show warning signs for hours before a collapse. Nurses are the staff most likely to see them. The ABCDE approach helps to assess in order of immediate danger:
Airway: is it clear?
Breathing: rate, effort and oxygen level.
Circulation: pulse, blood pressure, skin and urine output.
Disability: level of consciousness and blood glucose.
Exposure: look at the whole body for bleeding, rashes or wounds, and keep the person warm.

Problems found at each step should be dealt with or escalated before moving on, following training and local protocol. Consciousness can be scored by AVPU (alert, voice, pain, unresponsive) or by the Glasgow Coma Scale, which runs from 3 to 15.

sections.heading: Early warning scores and escalation
sections.text:
Early warning scores turn vital signs into a number, and a higher number prompts a defined response. In the UK, the National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2) is widely used. Other countries and hospitals use different tools. A score does not replace judgement. If you are worried, escalate, even if the score is low. A family member’s concern that the person is not right can also be an important clue.

Escalation should be clear and prompt. SBAR helps. If no response comes, follow the chain of command.

sections.heading: Shock and sepsis
sections.text:
Shock is a state in which tissues do not receive enough oxygen. It may be caused by blood or fluid loss, heart failure, severe infection or severe allergy. Early signs include a fast pulse, fast breathing, cold skin, reduced urine and confusion. Low blood pressure may appear late.

Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection. People may be confused, breathless or have a fever or low temperature. Sepsis is time-critical, and many facilities have a protocol. Anaphylaxis is a severe allergic reaction, and it is also an emergency with its own protocol. Resuscitation guidelines come from national and international councils and are updated regularly, so keep your training current.

keyPoints: ABCDE assesses in order of immediate danger.
Early warning scores support but do not replace judgement.
Escalate if you are worried, even if the score is low.
Low blood pressure can be a late sign of shock.
Sepsis is a time-critical emergency.

en.title: Palliative and end-of-life care
en.short: Comfort, communication, symptoms and grief in serious illness and at the end of life.

sections.heading: What palliative care is
sections.text:
Palliative care aims to improve the quality of life of people with serious illness, and of their families. It addresses physical, psychological, social and spiritual suffering. It is not only for the last days of life. It can start early, alongside treatment aimed at the disease. WHO considers it part of health care that all countries should provide, although access remains unequal.

Cicely Saunders, a founder of the modern hospice movement in the UK, described total pain. This means that suffering has physical, emotional, social and spiritual parts, and each part can make the others worse.

sections.heading: Comfort and symptoms
sections.text:
Common symptoms include pain, breathlessness, nausea, constipation, tiredness, confusion and anxiety. Nurses assess symptoms regularly and report them, give prescribed medicines safely, and provide mouth care, positioning, skin care and calm surroundings. Strong pain medicines are essential in this care, but many countries have limited supplies, or fears about their use. Prescribing and control of such medicines follow national law and guidelines.

Much palliative care happens at home, often with family carers. In many African communities, relatives and faith leaders play a large part. Nurses can teach families, and they can support carers, who may become exhausted.

sections.heading: Communication, wishes and grief
sections.text:
People have different preferences about how much to know and who should be told. Ask gently, listen, and do not guess. Many countries have laws about advance care planning, so check what applies. Religious and cultural customs around death are important, and these include how the body is cared for. Ask the family what they would like.

Grief is the natural response to loss. Elisabeth Kübler-Ross described denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance, but people do not move through these in a fixed order. Some grief can continue for a long time. Nurses also feel loss, so team support and reflection help them to continue working well.

keyPoints: Palliative care can begin early in a serious illness.
Total pain includes physical, emotional, social and spiritual parts.
Ask about preferences rather than assuming them.
Family carers need support too.
Grief does not follow a fixed order.

en.title: Maternal health: antenatal care
en.short: Care during pregnancy, the WHO contact model, estimating the due date and danger signs.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text:
Maternal health is a major concern worldwide. WHO estimates that about 260,000 women died from pregnancy-related causes in 2023, and most of these deaths occurred in low-income and lower-middle-income countries, especially in sub-Saharan Africa. Leading causes include severe bleeding, high blood pressure, infection, unsafe abortion and complications of delivery such as obstructed labour. Most of these deaths are preventable with timely, skilled care.

WHO’s 2016 guidance recommends at least eight antenatal contacts, with the first in the first 12 weeks. National programmes may differ. Each contact is a chance to assess, screen, teach and build trust.

sections.heading: Assessment terms
sections.text:
Gravida is the number of pregnancies, including the current one. Para is usually the number of births past a set point in pregnancy. That point differs between systems, for example 24 weeks in the UK, so check your local definition.

Naegele’s rule estimates the due date from the first day of the last menstrual period: add seven days, then subtract three months, and adjust the year.
Example: a period starting on 10 March 2025 gives about 17 December 2025.
The rule assumes regular 28-day cycles, so early ultrasound gives a better estimate where available.

Care commonly includes measuring blood pressure, testing urine, checking for anaemia, measuring the height of the uterus, listening to the fetal heart and screening for infections such as HIV and syphilis. Prevention measures, such as tetanus vaccine and malaria prevention in endemic areas, follow national guidelines.

sections.heading: Danger signs
sections.text: Women should be taught to seek help immediately for vaginal bleeding, severe headache or blurred vision, convulsions, fever, severe abdominal pain, leaking fluid or reduced fetal movement. Pre-eclampsia is new high blood pressure after 20 weeks of pregnancy, with protein in the urine or signs of organ damage. It can progress to convulsions, which is called eclampsia. Local protocols guide management. Respectful care means privacy, kindness, consent and freedom from discrimination, and these improve the use of services.

keyPoints: WHO recommends at least eight antenatal contacts.
Gravida counts pregnancies; definitions of para vary.
Naegele’s rule adds seven days and subtracts three months.
Pre-eclampsia starts after 20 weeks of pregnancy.
Teach danger signs at every contact.

en.title: Midwifery basics: labour and birth
en.short: The stages of labour, monitoring progress, respectful care, and the three delays model.

sections.heading: Stages of labour
sections.text:
Midwifery is the profession concerned with care of women through pregnancy, labour, birth and the time after birth, along with care of the newborn. Labour is usually described in stages:
First stage: from regular contractions to full dilatation of the cervix. It has a latent phase and an active phase.
Second stage: from full dilatation to birth of the baby.
Third stage: from birth of the baby to delivery of the placenta.
Some textbooks add a fourth stage, the first hours after the placenta is delivered.

Progress depends on the contractions, the shape of the pelvis and the position of the baby. WHO’s 2018 guidance places the start of the active first stage at about 5 cm, rather than the older 4 cm. Some national programmes still use older definitions.

sections.heading: Monitoring and care
sections.text: The partograph has long been used to record progress in labour. In 2020, WHO published the Labour Care Guide, which adds attention to the woman’s comfort, companionship and preferences. The aim is to spot problems early without unnecessary intervention. Labour companions, freedom of movement where possible, and respectful communication are all part of good care.

sections.heading: Bleeding and delay
sections.text:
Postpartum haemorrhage is heavy bleeding after birth and is a leading cause of maternal death worldwide. A loss of 500 mL or more has been the common definition. Guidance from WHO, FIGO and ICM in 2025 advises acting earlier, at about 300 mL when there are abnormal signs such as a fast pulse. Check your current national guideline. Active management of the third stage, using a uterotonic medicine under protocol, helps to prevent it.

The three delays model, from Thaddeus and Maine in 1994, explains why women die: delay in deciding to seek care, delay in reaching a facility, and delay in receiving good care. Midwives work to reduce all three, with birth plans, transport plans, early referral and emergency readiness. This summary teaches concepts. Practice requires supervised training and current protocols.

keyPoints: Labour has three main stages, and some books add a fourth.
WHO places the active first stage from about 5 cm.
The Labour Care Guide was published by WHO in 2020.
Postpartum haemorrhage is a leading cause of maternal death.
The three delays are deciding, reaching and receiving care.

en.title: Postnatal and newborn care
en.short: Care of mother and baby after birth: the first hour, Apgar score, feeding and danger signs.

sections.heading: The first hour
sections.text:
Immediate skin-to-skin contact helps to keep the baby warm and helps start breastfeeding. WHO advises that breastfeeding begin within the first hour, and be exclusive for about six months, with continued breastfeeding alongside other foods afterwards. Where a mother has an illness or takes medicines, she should receive individual advice.

The Apgar score assesses a newborn at one and five minutes, using five signs: colour, heart rate, reflex response, muscle tone and breathing. Each is scored 0, 1 or 2, giving a total out of 10. It describes the baby’s condition at that time. A baby who is not breathing needs help at once, and resuscitation does not wait for the score. Other routine newborn care, such as eye care, vitamin K and vaccines, follows national guidelines.

sections.heading: The mother after birth
sections.text:
WHO’s 2022 guidance recommends at least four postnatal contacts: in the first 24 hours, at 48 to 72 hours, at 7 to 14 days and in week six. Nurses and midwives check bleeding, the shrinking of the uterus (involution), the discharge called lochia, the perineum or wound, passing urine and breastfeeding. Danger signs include heavy bleeding, fever, foul-smelling discharge, severe headache, chest pain, and pain or swelling in a leg.

Mental health needs care too. Mild tearfulness is common in the first days and usually passes soon. Postpartum depression lasts longer and affects daily life. Postpartum psychosis is rare, and it is a psychiatric emergency that needs immediate help. Partners and relatives should know where to get local help. Any woman who feels unwell or unsafe should seek medical help without delay.

sections.heading: Newborn danger signs
sections.text: Mothers should learn to seek urgent care if a baby feeds poorly, has convulsions, breathes fast or with difficulty, is too hot or too cold, moves less than expected or looks yellow in the first day. Cord care advice varies between settings. Keep advice consistent with national guidance.

keyPoints: Skin-to-skin contact supports warmth and breastfeeding.
WHO advises exclusive breastfeeding for about six months.
The Apgar score is taken at one and five minutes.
WHO’s 2022 guidance recommends at least four postnatal contacts.
Postpartum psychosis is an emergency.

en.title: Reproductive and sexual health nursing
en.short: Family planning counselling, sexually transmitted infections, cervical screening and gender-based violence.

sections.heading: Family planning counselling
sections.text:
Family planning helps people to decide whether and when to have children. It improves the health of women and children. Methods include barrier methods, hormonal pills and injections, implants, intrauterine devices, fertility awareness methods and permanent procedures. They differ in effectiveness, side effects and how they are used. Condoms are the only method that also reduces the spread of sexually transmitted infections.

Good counselling gives accurate information, respects the person’s values and supports a free choice. It protects privacy, without pressure from the nurse. WHO publishes medical eligibility criteria that help decide which methods are safe for different people, and these are used alongside national guidance. Laws and services differ between countries.

sections.heading: Infections and screening
sections.text: Sexually transmitted infections, such as syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia and HIV, can cause serious harm and many have no symptoms. Testing, partner notification and treatment follow national guidelines, and are confidential. Cervical cancer is linked to persistent infection with human papillomavirus (HPV). It can be prevented by HPV vaccination and by screening, which finds changes before cancer develops. Vaccine and screening programmes differ between countries.

sections.heading: Violence, harmful practices and abortion care
sections.text:
Nurses may be the first to notice gender-based violence. WHO’s first-line support is summarised as LIVES: Listen, Inquire about needs, Validate, Enhance safety and Support. Speak privately, avoid blame, record carefully and follow local reporting law. Female genital mutilation is a harmful practice with no health benefit and is illegal in many countries. Nurses should never perform it, and should provide care with sensitivity to those affected.

Laws on abortion differ widely between countries. Nurses need to know their own country’s law. Whatever the law, care for complications after abortion or miscarriage is essential health care, and should be given without judgement.

Anyone who has been assaulted, is unsafe or has symptoms of an infection should seek help from a local health service or a trusted support service. These notes do not replace that help.

keyPoints: Family planning counselling supports free, informed choice.
Condoms also reduce the spread of sexually transmitted infections.
Vaccination and screening help to prevent cervical cancer.
LIVES summarises first-line support after violence.
Care after abortion or miscarriage is given without judgement.

en.title: Child health: growth, nutrition and immunisation
en.short: Child development, growth monitoring, malnutrition, immunisation programmes and the cold chain.

sections.heading: Growth and development
sections.text:
Growth means an increase in size, and development means a gain in skills. Nurses track both. Growth charts, such as the WHO child growth standards, compare a child’s weight and height with reference values. A single point says little, and the direction of the line says more. Development is assessed in motor, language, social and thinking skills. Parents can report milestones. For example, many babies sit without help by about six to nine months. A child who loses skills, or who is well behind, should be referred.

Theorists such as Piaget and Erikson describe stages in thinking and in social development. These help nurses to talk with children at the right level.

sections.heading: Nutrition
sections.text: Good nutrition in the first 1,000 days, from conception to age two, has lasting effects. Malnutrition includes stunting (low height for age), wasting (low weight for height) and overweight. Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is a quick screening measure in young children, and severe acute malnutrition needs specialised care. Nurses teach about breastfeeding, safe complementary foods from about six months, and hygiene. They should give advice with care, respecting family resources and local foods.

sections.heading: Immunisation
sections.text:
Vaccines train the immune system to recognise an infection. WHO’s Expanded Programme on Immunization began in 1974. Schedules differ between countries and change, so use your national schedule.

The cold chain is the system that keeps vaccines at the correct temperature from factory to patient. A break can make a vaccine ineffective, and heat or freezing damage may not be visible. Vaccine vial monitors and temperature records help. Nurses keep accurate records and explain expected side effects, such as mild fever and a sore arm. An adverse event following immunisation (AEFI) should be reported through the national system. Listen to parents’ concerns about vaccines, and answer with clear, honest information rather than blame.

keyPoints: Growth is size; development is skill.
The direction of the growth line matters more than one point.
Stunting is low height for age; wasting is low weight for height.
Immunisation schedules differ between countries.
The cold chain protects vaccine quality.
Report adverse events following immunisation.

en.title: Paediatric nursing: the sick child
en.short: Family-centred care, IMCI danger signs, child-specific safety and sickle cell disease.

sections.heading: Children are not small adults
sections.text:
Children differ from adults in body size, physiology and understanding. Their airways are narrow, so a small swelling can cause a large obstruction. They can become dehydrated more quickly, and they may compensate well and then worsen suddenly. Normal vital signs vary with age, so use age-appropriate charts.

Family-centred care recognises the family as a partner in care. Hospital stays can frighten children. Honest explanation at the child’s level, play and a parent’s presence all reduce distress. Older children and adolescents should be included in decisions as far as they are able. Laws on the consent of minors differ between countries.

sections.heading: Assessing the sick child
sections.text:
Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) is a WHO and UNICEF approach for first-level health workers. It checks for general danger signs in children aged two months to five years: unable to drink or breastfeed, vomiting everything, convulsions, and being lethargic or unconscious. Any of these needs urgent attention and usually referral. It also uses simple measures. Fast breathing, for example, is 50 breaths per minute or more from 2 to 12 months, and 40 or more from 12 months to 5 years. Pneumonia, diarrhoea and malaria remain leading causes of death in young children in many countries. Oral rehydration has saved many lives in diarrhoea.

Children’s doses are often based on weight, so a small error can be serious. Accurate weight and independent checks are essential. National IMCI charts should be followed.

sections.heading: Sickle cell disease and protection
sections.text:
Sickle cell disease is an inherited disorder of haemoglobin. Nigeria has the largest number of affected births in the world. Red cells become sickle-shaped, which causes anaemia, painful crises and infection risk. Triggers may include dehydration, cold and infection. Nurses take pain seriously, support families and teach when to seek urgent care. Genetic counselling and newborn screening are important where available.

Nurses also have a duty to safeguard children. Signs of abuse or neglect must be raised under local policy.

keyPoints: Children can compensate well, then worsen suddenly.
IMCI lists four general danger signs.
Children’s medicine errors can be serious, so accurate weight is essential.
Sickle cell disease is inherited and causes painful crises.
Safeguarding children is a duty of every nurse.

en.title: Mental health nursing: foundations
en.short: Mental health and stigma, the therapeutic relationship, mental state assessment, rights and law.

sections.heading: Understanding mental health
sections.text:
Mental health is more than the absence of illness. It includes coping with stress, working and contributing to a community. Mental health conditions are common worldwide, and they are influenced by biology, psychology and social factors, which is called the biopsychosocial model. Stigma often stops people from seeking help, and it can lead to neglect or abuse. Careful language puts the person first: for example, a person living with schizophrenia.

The recovery approach holds that people can live meaningful lives with or without continuing symptoms. WHO’s mental health gap programme (mhGAP) supports care by non-specialists in places with few specialists.

sections.heading: The therapeutic relationship and assessment
sections.text:
The nurse’s main tool in mental health care is the relationship with the person. It is built on trust, consistency, respect and clear boundaries.

The mental state examination describes the person’s presentation at one point in time. It commonly covers appearance and behaviour, speech, mood and affect, thought, perception, cognition and insight. Risk assessment considers possible harm to self, harm to others, and vulnerability to harm from others. Physical health also matters. People with severe mental illness often die earlier from physical conditions, so nurses should monitor physical health too.

sections.heading: Rights and law
sections.text:
Mental health law differs between countries. Most laws describe when a person may be treated without consent, with safeguards. Examples include Nigeria’s national mental health law, signed in January 2023, Ghana’s Mental Health Act 2012 and South Africa’s Mental Health Care Act of 2002. In England and Wales, the Mental Health Act 1983 is being amended by the Mental Health Act 2025, in stages. Use the current law where you work.

Capacity and consent must be considered for each decision. Having a mental illness does not automatically mean a person cannot decide. Traditional and faith healers are important in many communities, and nurses should discuss them with respect, while protecting people from harm or abuse, such as being chained. Anyone unwell or in crisis should seek local medical help.

keyPoints: The biopsychosocial model considers biology, psychology and social factors.
The therapeutic relationship is the nurse’s main tool.
The mental state examination describes one point in time.
Mental illness does not automatically remove capacity.
Mental health law differs between countries.

en.title: Mental health nursing: common conditions and crisis
en.short: Depression, anxiety, psychosis, substance use and dementia, with safe responses to suicide risk.

sections.heading: Common conditions
sections.text:
Depression involves persistent low mood or loss of interest, often with sleep and appetite changes, poor concentration and feelings of worthlessness. Anxiety disorders involve excessive worry or fear that affects daily life. Schizophrenia is a psychotic disorder, which may include delusions, hallucinations and disorganised thinking. Bipolar disorder includes periods of raised mood and often periods of depression. Substance use disorders involve continued use despite harm. Dementia causes progressive loss of memory and other mental abilities, and it should be distinguished from delirium, which starts suddenly and often has a physical cause such as infection.

Diagnosis is made by qualified professionals, using systems such as ICD-11 and DSM-5-TR.

sections.heading: Treatment concepts
sections.text: Care commonly combines psychological therapy, social support and, where indicated, medicines. Classes include antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood stabilisers and anxiolytics. Nurses monitor benefit and side effects, such as movement problems, weight gain or sedation, and they report concerns. Support for adherence means understanding the person’s reasons, not forcing agreement. Medicines should not be stopped suddenly without advice. Choices and doses belong to the prescriber and national guidelines, so these notes do not give them.

sections.heading: Suicide risk and crisis
sections.text:
Asking directly about suicidal thoughts does not plant the idea, and it can bring relief. Nurses should listen without judgement, ask about thoughts and plans, and take all statements seriously. They should not leave a person at immediate risk alone, and they should escalate urgently using local policy. Reducing access to means of harm is an effective way to prevent suicide. Follow-up after discharge matters.

If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide or feels unsafe, contact local emergency services or a nearby clinic or hospital now, or tell a trusted person.

When a person is very agitated, de-escalation comes first. Use a calm voice, give space, listen and offer choices. Restraint and seclusion are last resorts with legal safeguards, because they can cause serious harm. Never use them as punishment or for convenience.

keyPoints: Delirium starts suddenly and often has a physical cause.
Diagnosis is made by qualified professionals.
Asking directly about suicide does not plant the idea.
Do not leave a person at immediate risk alone.
De-escalation comes first, and restraint is a last resort.
Anyone in crisis should seek local help now.

en.title: Community and public health nursing
en.short: Primary health care, levels of prevention, basic epidemiology, home visits and health education.

sections.heading: Primary health care
sections.text:
Community nursing cares for people where they live, and it treats the community itself as the client. Primary health care (PHC) is the first level of contact with the health system. The Declaration of Alma-Ata in 1978 set it out as the route to health for all, and the Declaration of Astana in 2018 renewed this. Its principles include equity, community participation, use of suitable technology and work across sectors.

Countries organise PHC differently. Examples include Ghana’s Community-based Health Planning and Services (CHPS) and community health workers in Kenya, South Africa and Nigeria. Health also depends on social determinants: income, education, housing, clean water, sanitation and safety.

sections.heading: Levels of prevention and epidemiology
sections.text:
Primary prevention stops disease before it starts, as vaccines and clean water do.
Secondary prevention finds disease early, as blood pressure screening does.
Tertiary prevention limits harm from existing disease, as rehabilitation after a stroke does.

Epidemiology studies the distribution and causes of health problems in populations. Incidence is the number of new cases in a period, relative to those at risk. Prevalence is the proportion of people who have a condition at a given time.

Example: in a town of 6,000 people, 30 new cases of a disease occur in one year, and no one had it before.
Incidence = 30 ÷ 6,000 = 5 per 1,000 people per year.

sections.heading: Community practice
sections.text: A community diagnosis gathers data and residents’ views to identify priorities, and the community helps to decide the action. Home visits let nurses see the real conditions of daily life, while respecting that they are guests. Health education should be two-way and culturally suitable. For example, a nurse in rural Uganda might plan with mothers and local leaders on safe water and handwashing, rather than simply giving a talk. Community nurses also help with immunisation, antenatal care, disease surveillance and reporting outbreaks to health authorities.

keyPoints: Alma-Ata in 1978 set out primary health care as the route to health for all.
PHC principles include equity and community participation.
Primary, secondary and tertiary prevention act at different stages.
Incidence counts new cases; prevalence counts existing cases.
Social determinants strongly influence health.

en.title: Nursing ethics
en.short: Ethical principles, informed consent, confidentiality and the ICN Code of Ethics.

sections.heading: Principles
sections.text:
Ethics asks what is right to do. Four widely taught principles come from Beauchamp and Childress:
Autonomy: respecting a person’s right to decide.
Beneficence: acting for the person’s good.
Non-maleficence: avoiding harm.
Justice: treating people fairly and sharing resources fairly.

Nurses also value truthfulness, confidentiality, fidelity (keeping promises) and advocacy. Different approaches can lead to different answers. Consequentialism focuses on outcomes, and deontology focuses on duties. Virtue ethics asks what a good nurse would be like. In some communities, decisions are made with the family, and this can be respected while still making sure that the person’s own wishes are heard.

sections.heading: Consent and confidentiality
sections.text:
Informed consent needs three elements: adequate information, capacity to decide and freedom from pressure. It may be spoken, written or implied, depending on the procedure and local rules. Agreement to one thing does not mean agreement to everything, and a person may change their mind. For a nurse, simple care still needs explanation and agreement.

Confidentiality protects trust. Exceptions exist, such as serious risk to others, a court order or a legal duty to report. These differ between countries, so nurses should seek advice from a senior or a professional body.

sections.heading: Codes and dilemmas
sections.text:
The International Council of Nurses (ICN) Code of Ethics for Nurses was revised in 2021. It has four elements: nurses and patients or other people requiring care or services, nurses and practice, nurses and the profession, and nurses and global health. National codes also apply.

A dilemma arises when duties conflict. For example, Aisha is an adult with capacity who refuses a recommended treatment, and her family asks the nurse to persuade her. The nurse should make sure she understands the choice, listen to her reasons, involve the team and respect her decision within the law. The nurse should record what happened. Pressure or deception would break trust. Discussing difficult cases with colleagues or an ethics committee can help.

keyPoints: The four principles are autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice.
Consent needs information, capacity and freedom from pressure.
Confidentiality has limited exceptions that vary by country.
The ICN Code was revised in 2021 and has four elements.
A dilemma arises when duties conflict.

en.title: Nursing law and regulation
en.short: Regulators such as the NMCN and their equivalents, scope of practice, negligence and records.
keywords: Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria

sections.heading: Regulators
sections.text:
A nursing regulator protects the public by setting standards for education and practice, keeping a register, and handling discipline. Examples:
Nigeria: the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria (NMCN), under the Nursing and Midwifery (Registration, etc.) Act, Cap N143, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria 2004, which dates from 1979. The Act also sets up a Nurses and Midwives Disciplinary Tribunal.
Ghana: the Nursing and Midwifery Council, under the Health Professions Regulatory Bodies Act 2013 (Act 857).
Kenya: the Nursing Council of Kenya, under the Nurses and Midwives Act (Cap 257).
South Africa: the South African Nursing Council, under the Nursing Act 33 of 2005.
UK: the Nursing and Midwifery Council, under the Nursing and Midwifery Order 2001, with its published Code.

These laws can be amended, so check the regulator’s website. A registered nurse must usually keep the licence current and meet any continuing education rules.

sections.heading: Scope and accountability
sections.text: Scope of practice describes what a nurse may lawfully do. It depends on the law, the regulator, training and the employer’s policy. A nurse is accountable for personal actions and omissions, even when following an instruction. If an instruction seems unsafe, the nurse should question it and escalate. A nurse who delegates a task remains accountable for the decision to delegate.

sections.heading: Negligence and records
sections.text:
In many common-law countries, negligence requires four things: a duty of care, a breach of that duty, harm, and a causal link between the breach and the harm. Details vary by country.

In the UK, Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board (2015) held that patients must be told of material risks and reasonable alternatives, which strengthened patient-centred consent. Other countries may differ.

Records may be used as evidence in court or at a tribunal. Accurate and timely notes protect both patients and nurses. Raising concerns about unsafe care is a professional duty, and some countries give legal protection to those who do so. These notes are for learning and are not legal advice.

keyPoints: Regulators keep registers, set standards and handle discipline.
In Nigeria, the NMCN operates under Cap N143 LFN 2004.
Nurses are accountable for their acts and omissions.
Negligence needs duty, breach, harm and a causal link.
Laws vary by country and can change.

en.title: Patient safety and quality improvement
en.short: How harm happens in health care, the just culture, incident reporting and improvement methods.

sections.heading: How harm happens
sections.text:
Patient safety means preventing avoidable harm during health care. WHO estimates that around one in ten patients is harmed in health care, and much of this harm can be prevented. WHO’s Global Patient Safety Action Plan 2021 to 2030 sets out a framework for national action. Common sources of harm include medicines, infections, surgery, falls, pressure injuries, diagnosis and poor handover.

James Reason’s Swiss cheese model describes a system’s defences as slices with holes. Harm occurs when holes line up. Active failures are errors by front-line staff. Latent conditions are weaknesses in the system, such as short staffing, poor labelling or similar packaging. Human factors is the study of how people interact with systems. It accepts that everyone makes mistakes, and it designs work to make errors less likely.

sections.heading: Reporting and learning
sections.text: An adverse event causes harm. A near miss would have caused harm but was caught in time. Both should be reported, as near misses teach lessons cheaply. A just culture separates honest error from reckless behaviour. It does not blame individuals for system faults, but it holds people accountable for choices. Root cause analysis investigates why an event occurred, not only who was involved. Being open with patients when things go wrong is an ethical duty, and in some countries it is also a legal one.

sections.heading: Improving quality
sections.text:
Avedis Donabedian described quality in terms of structure (resources), process (what is done) and outcomes (results). Improvement often uses the Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycle, which tests a small change and learns from it.

Example: a ward in Accra records many missed fluid charts.
Plan: a nurse keeps a chart at each bedside for two weeks.
Do: the team tries it on six beds.
Study: audit shows fewer missed entries.
Act: the team adjusts the plan and extends it to other beds.

Safety also depends on speaking up. Every nurse should feel able to pause a task or question a senior when something seems wrong.

keyPoints: Harm is usually caused by systems as well as individuals.
The Swiss cheese model describes failed layers of defence.
Report near misses as well as adverse events.
A just culture separates honest error from recklessness.
Donabedian’s model is structure, process and outcomes.
PDSA means Plan, Do, Study, Act.

en.title: Nursing leadership and management
en.short: Leadership styles, delegation, staffing, managing change and conflict, and simple budgeting.

sections.heading: Leading and managing
sections.text:
Management focuses on planning, organising, staffing and control. Leadership focuses on setting direction and inspiring others. Common styles are:
Autocratic: the leader decides alone. This may suit an emergency.
Democratic: the leader involves the team.
Laissez-faire: the leader gives little direction.
Transformational: the leader motivates through a shared vision and supports staff to grow.
