No style suits every situation. Good leaders adapt and they protect a safe environment for patients and staff.

sections.heading: Delegation and staffing
sections.text:
Delegation means giving another person the authority to do a task, while the delegator remains accountable for the decision. Many courses teach five rights of delegation: the right task, circumstance, person, direction and supervision. Delegation must stay within the law and within each person’s training.

Staffing affects safety. Research in several countries links better nurse staffing to fewer deaths, but safe levels depend on the setting and patients.

Example of staffing arithmetic:
A ward has 24 patients who need an average of 6 nursing hours per patient per day.
24 × 6 = 144 hours per day.
With 12-hour shifts: 144 ÷ 12 = 12 shifts to cover each day.
This is only a planning figure, and it does not include leave or sickness.

sections.heading: Change, conflict and resources
sections.text:
Kurt Lewin’s model of change has three steps: unfreeze, change and refreeze. A leader explains why a change is needed, supports people through it, then makes it part of normal work. Conflict is common in busy teams. Addressing it early, in private, and with a focus on the problem usually works better than avoiding it.

Managers also control resources. For example, if a ward uses 40 boxes of gloves a month at ₦4,500 per box, it spends 40 × ₦4,500 = ₦180,000 per month. If supplies fall short, the manager should raise the risk formally rather than ask staff to work unsafely. Leaders also support staff wellbeing, mentoring and professional growth, which help to keep nurses in the workforce.

keyPoints: Management organises; leadership gives direction.
No single leadership style suits every situation.
The delegator stays accountable for the decision to delegate.
Lewin’s steps are unfreeze, change and refreeze.
Better nurse staffing has been linked to better outcomes.

en.title: Advanced nursing practice
en.short: Advanced practice roles, what makes practice advanced, and how law and titles differ between countries.

sections.heading: What advanced practice means
sections.text: Advanced practice nursing refers to expert knowledge, complex decision-making and extended clinical skills, usually gained through education beyond the first registration. The ICN published guidelines in 2020 that describe two main roles. The clinical nurse specialist usually focuses on expert care for a group of patients or a specialty, and on improving nursing and systems. The nurse practitioner usually provides direct care with greater autonomy, which may include assessment, diagnosis and treatment within the law. The guidelines treat a master’s degree as the minimum standard of preparation for these roles, but countries are at different stages.

sections.heading: Titles and law differ
sections.text: Titles and authority vary widely. In the United States, advanced practice registered nurses include nurse practitioners, clinical nurse specialists, nurse-midwives and nurse anaesthetists, and state laws differ. In the UK, many services use a framework for advanced clinical practice with four pillars: clinical practice, leadership and management, education and research. In many African countries, advanced roles are developing. Some nurses extend their practice through national task-shifting policies, as with HIV care, or through specialist primary care roles. Authority to diagnose or prescribe depends on national law. Never assume that a title gives the same rights in another country.

sections.heading: Competencies and evaluation
sections.text:
An advanced practitioner is expected to show:
Advanced assessment and clinical reasoning, including uncertainty and complex needs.
Ethical decision-making and awareness of the limits of personal competence.
Leadership and work across professions.
Use and production of evidence.
Teaching and support of other nurses.

The value of such roles should be evaluated rather than assumed. Research often considers access, patient outcomes, satisfaction and cost. A master’s student might compare a nurse-led hypertension clinic in Nairobi with usual care, using blood pressure control, follow-up rates and cost in shillings. Important questions include the training and supervision of staff, the supply of medicines and whether the role is sustainable. Policy discussion is needed so that roles are clearly defined and safely regulated.

keyPoints: ICN describes two main roles: clinical nurse specialist and nurse practitioner.
ICN guidelines set a master’s degree as the minimum standard for these roles.
Titles and prescribing rights depend on national law.
UK frameworks use four pillars of advanced practice.
New roles should be evaluated, not assumed to work.

en.title: Evidence-based nursing
en.short: Asking clinical questions with PICO, searching, appraising evidence and putting it into practice.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text:
Evidence-based nursing combines the best available research, clinical expertise and the values and circumstances of the patient. It does not mean following research alone. A common process is: ask, acquire, appraise, apply and assess.

A focused question often uses PICO: Population, Intervention, Comparison and Outcome.
Example: In older adults in hospital (P), does hourly nurse rounding (I), compared with usual care (C), reduce falls (O)?

Searches use databases such as CINAHL, PubMed and the Cochrane Library, with planned keywords and limits. Where access is limited, WHO’s Hinari programme can help eligible institutions in lower-income countries.

sections.heading: Appraising evidence
sections.text:
Evidence is often shown as a hierarchy. Systematic reviews and randomised controlled trials stand high for questions about the effects of treatment, while cohort and case-control studies follow. Qualitative research best answers questions about experience. So the best design depends on the question. Critical appraisal asks whether a study is valid, what the results show and whether they apply here. Tools from the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) support this. The GRADE system rates certainty in a body of evidence.

Example of effect sizes:
A complication occurs in 20% of the control group and 15% of the intervention group.
Absolute risk reduction = 20% − 15% = 5%.
Number needed to treat = 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20.
So about 20 people must receive the intervention for one to benefit, on these figures.

sections.heading: Moving evidence into practice
sections.text:
Good evidence often takes years to reach practice. Implementation science studies this gap. Barriers include limited time, resources and authority, and resistance to change. Facilitators include supportive leaders, local champions, audit and feedback, and simple guidelines.

Evidence must also fit the setting. A study from a high-income hospital may not apply directly to a rural clinic in Ghana, because staffing and supplies differ. A good implementer adapts delivery without losing the essential elements, then measures the results. Always check that a guideline is recent, credible and approved in your country.

keyPoints: Evidence-based nursing combines research, expertise and patient values.
PICO means Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome.
The best study design depends on the question.
Number needed to treat is 1 divided by absolute risk reduction.
Evidence must be adapted to the setting.

en.title: Nursing research methods
en.short: Quantitative, qualitative and mixed designs, sampling, statistics, ethics and reporting standards.

sections.heading: Choosing a design
sections.text:
Research starts with a clear question and a review of existing work. Quantitative research measures variables and tests relationships. Designs include randomised controlled trials, quasi-experiments, cohort, case-control and cross-sectional studies. Qualitative research explores meaning and experience, using interviews, focus groups or observation. Approaches include phenomenology, grounded theory and ethnography. Mixed methods combine both for a fuller answer.

For example, a master’s student in Enugu asks how nurses feel about night shift work. A qualitative design fits. If she asks what proportion of nurses report burnout, a survey fits better.

sections.heading: Quality of data
sections.text:
In quantitative work, validity asks whether a tool measures what it claims to measure, and reliability asks whether it measures consistently. Probability sampling, such as random sampling, supports generalisation to a population. Convenience sampling is easier but has more risk of bias. A sample size calculation helps ensure that the study has enough power to detect a meaningful effect. A p-value indicates how likely results at least this extreme would be if there were truly no effect. A confidence interval shows the range of plausible values, and it is often more informative. Statistical significance does not prove clinical importance.

In qualitative work, Lincoln and Guba’s trustworthiness criteria are often used: credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability. Sampling is usually purposive. Thematic analysis, as described by Braun and Clarke, is one common way to analyse the data, and reflexivity means examining how the researcher’s own views may affect it.

sections.heading: Ethics and reporting
sections.text:
Research with people requires ethics review, informed consent, confidentiality and care for vulnerable groups. The Declaration of Helsinki is the best-known international statement of principles. Each country has its own review structures, such as Nigeria’s National Health Research Ethics Committee. Nurses who recruit their own patients should avoid any pressure on them to take part.

Reporting guidelines improve clarity: CONSORT for trials, STROBE for observational studies, COREQ for qualitative interviews and focus groups, and PRISMA for systematic reviews.

keyPoints: Match the design to the question.
Validity is accuracy; reliability is consistency.
Confidence intervals are often more informative than p-values.
Trustworthiness is used to judge qualitative work.
Ethics review and informed consent are required for research with people.
CONSORT, STROBE, COREQ and PRISMA guide reporting.
